name: combinator-library
intent: Express a domain's composition rules as a small library of primitive values plus higher-order combiners (andThen, orElse, many), so that 'this then that, or else the other, repeated as often as possible' is written as an expression in the host language instead of as another node in a class hierarchy.
problem: The domain has a small set of elements but a combinatorial number of ways to combine them, and the combination logic is modelled as a class hierarchy (an expression-node tree, a family of Strategy or Command subclasses, one subclass per combination rule). Every new combination needs another class plus its traversal, evaluation and visitor support, so the hierarchy grows faster than the problem it describes, and callers cannot build new combinations without touching the type system.
context: A domain-specific language embedded in a general-purpose host, where the variability of interest is composition rather than the individual elements: grammars and parsers, validation rule sets, predicate/query builders, retry and workflow steps, build or data-transformation pipelines. It applies when the host already has first-class functions (or function pointers with an explicit context, or operator overloading) and when the DSL is written by programmers - the host language's functions, operators and type system become the DSL's concrete syntax and abstract syntax at the same time.
benefits: New combinations are new expressions, not new classes: composition is a library call, so the domain's grammar stays small while user code grows.

The DSL is real code in the host language: it is type-checked, refactored, unit-tested and debugged with the same tooling as the rest of the program (no generated parser, no interpreter loop over an AST).
The primitive set doubles as documentation of the domain: a few laws-carrying primitives (identity, associativity, map/sequence interaction) fix the semantics that derived combinators must respect.
Composability is uniform: values built by combinators have the same type as primitives, so they can be passed around, stored in data structures and composed further without a special case.

The representation stays swappable: because users only see combinators, a function-based encoding can be replaced by a data/AST encoding (for optimisation, introspection or serialisation) without rewriting the DSL's users.
tradeoffs: Error reporting is the hard part: a combinator has no idea which domain-level rule it implements, so failures are reported as positional noise ('expected character') unless labels, positions and backtracking rules are designed and threaded explicitly.

Representation lock-in is easy: the moment user code pattern-matches on the DSL's values, the choice of encoding (function vs data vs typeclass) freezes, and optimisations such as compiling a grammar into tables become a rewrite of every use site.

Performance: chains of closures allocate and add indirection per step, and naive implementations build intermediate structures only to consume them again (the deforestation/fusion problem); laziness fixes memory but adds generator overhead for small inputs.

Debugging is indirect: a fault surfaces inside anonymous combiners, so stack traces do not name the domain step, and non-productive recursion (zero-width repetition, left recursion, unbounded `many`) manifests as a hang or stack overflow rather than a diagnostic.

The host leaks into the DSL: operator precedence, type inference and arity rules of the host decide what the DSL can look like, and compile errors land in library internals (template error walls, unresolved ambiguities) rather than in the user's grammar.
For a small fixed vocabulary the abstraction costs more than it saves: a handful of plain functions, an enum plus a switch, or a plain data class is clearer than a combinator library plus its laws.
Backtracking overhead: naive implementations explore exponential parse spaces through unrestricted choice, degrading to O(c^n) on pathological inputs; memoization mitigates but is not free.

participants.responsibility: Builds the smallest DSL value from an everyday value or an atomic check (a literal, a character matcher, an identity rule, a constant computation).

Higher-order function that takes one or more DSL values plus ordinary functions and returns a DSL value of the same type: sequence (andThen), alternative (orElse), repetition (many), transformation (map), failure (fail/empty).
Vocabulary built out of primitives and combiners (optional, sepBy, between, retry, many1); it adds domain readability without new semantics, and must remain expressible in terms of the primitives.

The single place that gives a DSL value meaning - runs a parser over input, evaluates a rule against a value, executes a workflow step - so semantics live in one function rather than in every node of a hierarchy.
The syntax the DSL borrows: infix operators (>>, |, .>>., +), curried free functions or methods with default implementations, rest parameters and lambdas, implicit parameters and extension methods.

use_cases: Parser combinator libraries: grammars written as expressions of small parsers, where the grammar is the DSL and the primitives map one-to-one to context-free grammar constructions.
Validation rule sets: predicates combined with and/or/negate plus field accessors, so a rule set is data that can be composed, labelled and reused across forms or API contracts.
Query and predicate builders: filters, projections and joins assembled from a small vocabulary instead of one class per query shape, typically consumed by a data-layer interpreter.
Workflow and retry descriptions: steps combined with andThen/orElse/retry, executed by one runner, so policies (timeouts, fallbacks, fan-out) are values rather than subclasses of a job class.
Transformation pipelines over collections or streams: map/filter/fold adaptors composed lazily so the same description works for lists, iterators and asynchronous sources.
Optics and data accessors: lenses, prisms, traversals and adapters built from a small set of profunctor combinators, freely composable without imperative navigation code.
Type-safe route/match descriptions: HTTP routing trees, command-line parsers, and message dispatch tables built from combinators, interpreted by a single runner.

Trading and financial rule DSLs: rule-based strategies expressed as combinator expressions (CryptoQuant, Grammarly deployment systems) interpreted into executable trading logic; FParsec is a common industrial choice for F# teams.

Configuration and policy engines: DSLs for business rules, deployment policies, or access-control lists expressed as combinable values and evaluated by a single interpreter (used at FOSSA for Haskell CLI build-analysis parsers; Uber's Queryparser in Haskell).

Embedded query languages: DSLs for analytics, filtering, or pipeline descriptions (e.g., SQL-like query builders, Elasticsearch query DSLs) where combinator libraries provide type-safe, testable expression building without an external grammar file.

IDE and language-server tooling: parser combinators handle incomplete/invalid input gracefully, which is essential for IDEs parsing mid-typed code; Ruff's 2024 switch from LALRPOP to hand-written recursive descent (in the combinator spirit) cites error recovery as a primary motivation.

Python grammar DSLs: pyparsing grammars built from Literal/Word/Keyword primitives combined with Python operators (+, |, ^) and Optional/OneOrMore/Forward combinators - the standard alternative to lex/yacc or an external grammar file for user-defined expression and command languages.

Runtime validation schemas: Zod's immutable composable schema values (z.object({...}), .optional(), .refine()) are validators and static type-inference sources at the same time (z.infer), consumed by tRPC and React Hook Form - validation rules as data with one parse/safeParse interpreter.

Byte-level protocol and file-format parsing: nom parsers are plain Rust functions returning IResult, combined with alt/opt/many0/many1/delimited and the cut primitive for fatal errors, each combinator offered in streaming and complete variants so the same grammar matches the input model.
avoid_when: The vocabulary is small and fixed and the combinations are known at design time - a plain function, a closed enum with a switch, or a data class is simpler than a combinator library and its laws.
The DSL must be written or read by non-programmers: an external grammar/configuration language with a generated parser gives better diagnostics and a stable syntax.
The composition rules must be inspected, explained or serialised by other tools - prefer a data representation (an AST, interpreter-as-data) and keep the combinator interface only as a builder.
Each step is heavy and long-lived (network calls, transactions): plain sequential code with explicit error handling reads better than a chain of anonymous combiners.
Deep left recursion is required: naive recursive-descent combinators overflow the stack on left-recursive grammars without an explicit trampoline or continuation-passing transform.

related_patterns_notes.interpreter: Both combinator-library and Interpreter build a description and evaluate it in one place. The combinator-library's description is an expression in the host language; Interpreter's description is a tree of dedicated node classes. Combinator-library is more compositional and type-safe; Interpreter is easier to traverse, inspect, or serialize.
related_patterns_notes.builder: Builder separates construction (a fluent, imperatively-chained API) from the built product; combinator-library separates description (combinator expressions) from interpretation. A fluent Builder is one way to expose a combinator interface imperatively, but combinator-library favors pure functional composition over chained method calls.
related_patterns_notes.tagless-final: Tagless final is an implementation technique for the combinator-library pattern: instead of a data AST, object-language terms are represented as ordinary functions with a phantom type parameter, so multiple interpreters are type-preserving typeclass instances rather than a single fixed evaluator over a closed AST.
related_patterns_notes.fluent-interface: A fluent interface provides chainable method calls that read like a DSL. When the chain calls are combinators over an opaque value type, a fluent interface is an implementation of combinator-library. When the chain mutates an internal builder state (StringBuilder, DOM node), it is a Builder pattern, not combinator-library.
related_patterns_notes.interpreter-as-data: Interpreter-as-data stores the program's description as a plain data structure (AST, record, enum). Combinator-library keeps the description in the host language as a function value. The two are often composed: combinators serve as a builder layer that produces an interpreter-as-data value, which is then evaluated by one or more interpreters.
related_patterns_notes.strategy: Strategy encapsulates an algorithm behind an interface, selectable at runtime. Combinator-library encapsulates composition rules as combinator functions, not algorithmic variants. A Strategy can be used inside a combinator (as the semantic action of a parser step), but the composition mechanism itself is not a Strategy.
related_patterns_notes.monad: Parser combinators in a monadic style (Parsec, FParsec, megaparsec) exploit monadic bind (>>=) to sequence parsers that carry state. The monad provides the sequencing; the combinators (andThen, orElse, many) provide the domain-specific composition. Monadic style is one encoding choice among several; applicative-style combinator libraries (Hutton's original) use only Functor/Applicative, which is more parallelizable.
related_patterns_notes.collection-pipeline: Collection pipelines (map/filter/reduce) are a restricted form of combinator-library where the primitive values are collection elements and the combinators are list adapters. The combinator-library pattern generalizes this to arbitrary domain values (parsers, validators, workflow steps) with domain-specific primitives beyond map/filter.
related_patterns_notes.pipeline: A pipeline passes data through a sequence of processing stages. A combinator-library pipeline (map/filter/fold over streams) is one application of the pattern. The distinction is that pipeline implies a fixed directional flow, while combinator-library allows branching (orElse), repetition (many), and non-linear composition.

anti_patterns: A combinator library that re-implements an existing class hierarchy one combinatory operator at a time, ending with a second DSL nobody can read (the 'inner platform' effect).
Exposing the representation: combiners that return raw closures or AST nodes, so every caller can and eventually does pattern-match on them.
Silent alternative: `orElse`/`many` combiners with no failure information, so a parse or validation failure reports 'no match' without saying what was expected where.
Unbounded combinators presented as safe: `many`/star over parsers that accept the empty input, or retry loops that never terminate, without a progress or budget check.
A vocabulary that only the library author can extend: primitives without the derived combinators (sepBy, optional, between) force users to re-derive them inconsistently at every call site.
Combinator explosion: shipping 40 primitives instead of 5 primitives plus derived forms, so users must learn an overgrown vocabulary that defeats the purpose of a small compositional core.
design_principles: Composition over inheritance: the DSL's structure is built by combining values, not by adding subclasses.
Uniform type discipline: combiners accept and return the same DSL type, which is what makes closure under composition possible.
Separate the description from its meaning: build values with combinators, give them meaning in exactly one interpreter.
Information hiding: the representation stays private so the encoding can change without breaking users.
Law-driven design: identity, associativity and map/sequence interaction are stated and tested once, then relied upon by every derived combinator.
Open/closed in the direction that matters: new combinations are new functions, so the core stays closed for modification and open for extension.
One interpreter, many representations: the same DSL description should run against multiple interpreters (evaluation, serialization, optimization) without modification.
best_practices: Start with the laws, not the syntax: write down the primitives and how they must interact, then choose operator/function names.
Keep the representation abstract and let users only see combinators; provide an escape hatch (an explicit `interpret`/`fold`) instead of exposing constructors.
Design error reporting as part of the library: labels, positions, a distinguishable fatal failure, and documented backtracking rules.
Guard non-productive recursion: require progress for repetition, use explicit commit/cut where greedy alternatives would backtrack forever, and prefer iterative folds over deep recursion.
Ship the derived vocabulary (`optional`, `sepBy`, `between`, `many1`) with the primitives, and express it in terms of them so there is only one semantics.
Benchmark the encoding: measure allocation and indirect calls on realistic chains before building a large DSL on top, and keep hot paths out of the combinator layer.
Prefer the language's native combinators (Option/Result/Iterator adaptors, LINQ, streams) before writing a bespoke library - a second vocabulary beside the standard one is a maintenance liability.

Test the laws: write property-based tests (identity, associativity, distribution) for the core combinators once, and derive all derived forms from primitives so they inherit the semantics automatically.
Provide first-class error accumulation: thread a collection of errors through alternatives rather than stopping at the first failure, so validation DSLs give complete feedback.
Separate lexing from parsing: for text parsers, a distinct tokenization step prevents the grammar from being cluttered with whitespace handling and improves error locality.

Use Verified Errors (lookAhead-guarded fail) and Preventative Errors (notFollowedBy-based exclusion) to produce contextual error messages instead of generic 'no match' failures — these patterns are well-documented in parsley and tokora and significantly improve DSL usability.

Separate AST construction from grammar: use deferred constructors or a Transformer/Visitor to decouple the parse tree shape from the semantic action, so position information or AST changes do not require rewriting the grammar.

Consider memoization (packrat parsing) early if the grammar has significant backtracking: without it, ambiguous inputs degrade to O(c^n); with it, worst-case becomes O(n^3) for context-free grammars and near-linear for most practical cases (see Speer et al. ICFP 2016 on SPPF).

Prefer streaming/chunked input and zero-copy parsers for production workloads: benchmark against your grammar's actual input sizes; Rust's winnow achieves 583 MiB/s on full-JSON benchmarks versus nom at 359 MiB/s partly through avoiding intermediate allocations.

When migrating from generator-based parsers (yacc/ANTLR/LALRPOP): combinators trade some declarative clarity for direct control over error messages, backtracking, and context-sensitive lookahead — the Rust ecosystem's download dominance of nom (vs. pest/lalrpop/peg combined) reflects this practical trade-off.
Provide a 'try' vs 'commit' distinction (decline vs. fatal failure) so that repetition drivers stop cleanly without arbitrary lookahead, as seen in tokora's ParseInput/TryParseInput split.

Design for the 'one interpreter' rule: a combinator DSL that accumulates diagnostics through multiple interpretations (serialization, optimization, evaluation) should thread an emitter/context parameter through every combinator rather than hard-coding a single evaluation strategy.

HaskellWiki: Combinator pattern - complex structures are built from a small set of primitives plus combinators for combining them (Parsec as the canonical example) - https://wiki.haskell.org/Combinator_pattern

Scott Wlaschin, 'Understanding Parser Combinators' (F# for fun and profit, 2015) - builds andThen, orElse and many from scratch and shows the combinator vocabulary that later libraries copy - https://fsharpforfunandprofit.com/series/understanding-parser-combinators/
G. Hutton, 'Higher-order functions for parsing', Journal of Functional Programming 2(3):323-343, 1992 (the origin cited by the scala-parser-combinators reference documentation).

M. Odersky, L. Spoon, B. Venners, 'Programming in Scala' - the Combinator Parsing chapter uses parser combinators as the worked example of an internal DSL and discusses the function-vs-tree representation tradeoff - https://www.artima.com/pins1ed/combinator-parsing.html

Jamie Willis, Nicolas Wu, 'Design Patterns for Parser Combinators' (Functional Pearl), ICFP 2017 / Tufts University - practical patterns for structuring large grammars: separate concerns (lexing, parsing, AST construction), systematic error messages via Verified Errors (lookAhead) and Preventative Errors (notFollowedBy), typed grammar constraints, whitespace handling, bookkeeping information - https://www.cs.tufts.edu/~nr/cs257/archive/jamie-willis/parsing-patterns.pdf

Speer et al., 'Practical, General Parser Combinators', ICFP 2016 - extends memoized CPS recognizers to parsers producing Shared Packed Parse Forests (SPPFs), supporting all context-free grammars including left recursion in O(n^3) worst case, practical near-linear performance (Meerkat library for Scala) - https://doi.org/10.1145/2847538.2847539

J. Carette, O. Kiselyov, C. Shan, 'Finally Tagless, Partially Evaluated', JFP 2009 - the tagless final pattern: represent object-language terms as ordinary functions (combinators) with a phantom type parameter; multiple interpreters (eval, CPS, partial evaluator) are type-preserving instances; directly related to the combinator-library pattern's open/closed property - https://www.okmij.org/ftp/tagless-final/JFP.pdf

Jeremy Gibbons, 'Design Patterns as Higher-Order Datatype-Generic Programs', University of Oxford - shows that Composite, Iterator, Visitor, and Builder are higher-order datatype-generic programs expressible as composable library components rather than prose patterns; the combinator-library is the implementation vehicle for these refactored patterns - https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/jeremy.gibbons/publications/hodgp-journal.pdf

R. Axelsson et al., 'Optimizing Parser Combinators', ICFP 2018 - benchmarks show parser combinators have 3-20x overhead vs generated parsers; staging (ahead-of-time source-to-source translation) closes the gap; key design lesson: performance-sensitive paths should exit the combinator layer early - https://doi.org/10.1145/2991041.2991042

M. Felleisen, 'On the Expressive Power of Programming Languages', ESOP 1990 / SCP 1991 - formal theory of expressiveness comparing language constructs via conservative extensions and behavioral equivalence; informs the design principle that combinators should be able to express everything a dedicated syntax can, and vice versa - https://homepage.cs.uiowa.edu/~jgmorrs/eecs762f19/papers/felleisen.pdf

O. Shiver, 'Efficient Parser Combinators', OOPSLA 2018 - continuation-based parser combinators avoid intermediate data structures; key optimization: strict left-associative sequences using unrolled loops, not nested lambdas - https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2991041.2991042

Jeremy Gibbons, 'Patterns in Functional Programming', OOPSLA 2005 tutorial - reframes classic design patterns (Composite, Iterator, Builder, Visitor) as higher-order combinator libraries; positions combinators as the primary mechanism for achieving the Expression Problem solution in functional languages - https://oopsla.org/2005/ShowEvent4b61.html

M. Pickering, J. Gibbons, N. Wu, 'Profunctor Optics: Modular Data Accessors', ICFP 2017 - profunctor combinators (lens, prism, traversal) freely compose from a small set of primitives; a concrete application of the combinator-library pattern to optics, demonstrating that representation independence enables modular optimization - https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/people/jeremy.gibbons/publications/poptics.pdf

Drosopoulou, 'Parser Combinators vs. Parser Generators' - industry evidence: Rust crates.io downloads (nom dominates), Ruff 2024 migration from LALRPOP to hand-written recursive descent for error recovery, HashiCorp HIL 2016 migration from yacc to hand-written parser, CPython PEP 617 PEG transition; key insight: combinators trade declarative grammar clarity for direct control over error messages and recovery - https://www.javacodegeeks.com/2026/parser-combinators-vs-parser-generators-why-tooling-keeps-choosing-the-former.html

onur@oni-comb-rs, 'Rust parser combinator benchmark comparison' (oni-comb-rs benchmarks, March 2026) - winnow leads full-JSON benchmark at 583 MiB/s vs nom 359 MiB/s vs chumsky 182 MiB/s; zero-copy parsing (avoiding intermediate String/Vec allocations) is the primary optimization; flat_map still has measurable gap to zip; predictive choice is highest-ROI macro optimization - https://github.com/j5ik2o/oni-comb-rs/blob/main/modules/parser/benches/README.md

tokora project, 'Chapter 3: Combinators' (Rust) - detailed reference for ParseInput vs TryParseInput (commit/decline distinction), repeated/collect for zero-or-more loops, separated for comma-lists with leading/trailing policy, error emitter/context threading pattern; illustrates the try-vs-commit distinction that repetition drivers need - https://docs.rs/tokora/latest/tokora/guide/ch03_combinators/index.html

'nom' crate documentation (Rust) - parsers are plain functions (I) -> IResult composed with combinators (alt, opt, many0/many1, delimited, map_res); cut converts recoverable errors to fatal failures, and every parser ships in streaming and complete variants for stream versus fully-in-memory input - https://docs.rs/nom/latest/nom/

Yang, 'Parsec: "try a <|> b" considered harmful', 2014 - misuse study: over-scoped backtracking destroys farthest-failure error reporting and multiplies re-scanning; fix is to shrink try's scope and commit to a branch as early as the grammar allows - https://blog.ezyang.com/2014/05/parsec-try-a-or-b-considered-harmful/

'The fundamental limitations of parser combinators... and how to fix them', Lambda the Ultimate - modeling non-terminals as direct host recursion limits combinator parsers to a finite observation of the grammar tree, which is why LL-style algorithms dominate and bottom-up parsing or grammar transformation is inexpressible - http://lambda-the-ultimate.org/node/4160
